extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, PR practitioners, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsels on analyzing problems, understanding publics, selecting media and tactics, and creating news and symbols to modify public opinion and behavior. Emphasizes appeals to instincts, use of stereotypes, timing with external conditions, and ethical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for changed external conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed external conditions must be taken into account by the public relations counsel in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes carry modifications in interests and points of view of those affected; the counsel must estimate what difference a medium or condition (e.g., radio, automobile, airplane, national prohibition, local edicts) will produce in any section of the public and either call attention to or interpret the change in terms of the interest of those affected. Examples: radio increases farmers' contact with world events; automobile removes isolation of country districts; align campaigns (e.g., thrift campaigns) with inflationary or other favorable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze client problem, public, and plan methods
rubrics_metrics.description: First he must analyze his client's problem and his client's objective. Then he must analyze the public he is trying to reach. He must devise a plan of action for the client to follow and determine the methods and the organs of distribution available for reaching his public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finally he must try to estimate the interaction between the public he seeks to reach and his client — how the client's case will strike the public mind. Example: When addressing a tariff bill, visualize multiple stakeholder perspectives to generalize appeals influential with many sections of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize multiple public perspectives / subgroup analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must see himself simultaneously as a member of a large number of publics and as member of subdivisions of each group (e.g., manufacturers who source domestically vs. from abroad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break publics into subdivisions by interest, geography, age, language, education, etc., to strike upon appeals influential with as many sections as possible; generalize from viewpoints to identify effective appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to instincts and universal desires
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal to the instincts and the universal desires is the basic method through which he produces his results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilize primary instincts (self-preservation, sex, hunger, parental love, curiosity, pugnacity, self-display, gregariousness, individualism, acquisition, construction) to craft messages. Examples: radiator ads appeal to shelter; food ads to gustatory sense; soap ads to sex appeal; use slogans ('Have you had your iron to-day?') to leverage self-preservation. Tailor appeals to particular instincts depending on the objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize and manage stereotypes and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel sometimes uses the current stereotypes, sometimes combats them and sometimes creates new ones. He must bring forward stereotypes the public knows to which he adds new ideas, or combat/replace harmful stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visible objects and emblems (flags, instruments, white factory walls) as physical metaphors that anchor vague human qualities; create new stereotypes (e.g., Roosevelt's 'square deal') or exploit favorable existing ones (Danube waltz for Austria). Beware of overuse ('shop-worn' stereotypes) and of substituting words for acts which demagogues may exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news by simplifying, dramatizing, and isolating ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract discussions and heavy facts cannot be given to the public until they are simplified and dramatized. When an appeal to the instincts can be made so powerful as to secure acceptance ... it can be aptly termed news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lift startling facts, isolate important and easily understandable points, develop ideas into events so they can claim attention as news. Treat analyses like headlines and cartoons — compact, vivid simplifications. The counsel is a creator of news for whatever medium he chooses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate mediums and anticipate medium effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is, of course, first and perhaps most important, the press. There is the moving picture; the lecture platform; there is advertising; there is the direct-by-mail effort; there is the stage; there is word of mouth; there is the pulpit, the schoolroom, the legislative chamber—to all of these the public relations counsel has distinct relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select media suited to the audience and message and estimate what difference the medium will produce in viewpoint (e.g., radio's effect on farmers). Consider each medium's reach, nature, and likely alteration of public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage group leaders and networks
rubrics_metrics.description: The gregarious instinct in man gives the public relations counsel the opportunity for his most potent work. A group leader gains such power with his group or herd that even on matters unrelated he is followed by his group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After analysis, subdivide publics and approach leaders (society leaders, political leaders, leaders of women, sportsmen, by geography, age, language, education). Enlist leaders with cross-cutting authority (e.g., presidents of multiple associations) to bring multiple groups into alignment. Use lists/vendors that supply group/leader contacts when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contest, issue, and pugnacity to attract attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity with its attendant emotion of anger is a human constant. The public relations counsel uses this continually in constructing events that call it into play; he stages battles against evils and creates issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize contests, debates, tests, or issues to create controversy and draw crowds (e.g., Cooper Union Forum experience, sporting contests). Recognize dangers: pugnacity can be enlisted for progress or used to suppress and oppress; employ responsibly. Examples: use of wartime metaphors in health campaigns ('kill the germs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Arouse curiosity and wonder (suspense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity and wonder are continually employed. In Governmental work ... feelers are often sent out to the public to help create curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teasers and advance signals to build interest before announcements; publishers use 'What is wrong with this picture?' type ads to stimulate wonder and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recognition and self-display to increase commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel utilizes the self-display-elation motive and draws public attention to particular people in groups, in order to give them a greater interest in the work they are espousing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public praise and naming opportunities (rooms, beds) can convert lukewarm supporters into active advocates. Use public recognition strategically to build leadership commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parental love and tenderness for charity and emotion-driven appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental love and tenderness are continually employed ... The whole flood of post-war charity-drives was keyed to this pitch. The starving Belgian orphan ... campaigns all succeeded on this issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy child imagery and appeals to parental instincts in fundraising and sympathy campaigns where ethically appropriate; these appeals are powerful and widespread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit habit and mental stereotypes as shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental habits create stereotypes just as physical habits create certain definite reflex actions. These stereotypes or reflex images are a great aid to the public relations counsel in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize pre-existing mental shortcuts (e.g., 'farmer' stereotype) to make messages more immediately comprehensible. Use, combat, or replace stereotypes deliberately, knowing they may not be truthful pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use play and public amusements to mobilize participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Play as an innate tendency is utilized ... When a charity committee is advised to institute a street fair to gather money ... a city government arranges fireworks ... the play tendency of human society finds an outlet and the initiators find friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize fairs, contests, spectacles, or games when conditions merit to draw public engagement via leisure/play instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft compact headlines and visual metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline is a compact, vivid simplification of complicated issues. The cartoon provides a visual image which takes the place of abstract thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop concise headline-like statements and strong visual imagery to encapsulate complex analyses and provoke immediate recognition and memory among the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize obscure public tendencies into symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the chief contribution of the public relations counsel ... is his capacity for crystallizing the obscure tendencies of the public mind before they have reached definite expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify nascent public sentiments, create symbols and slogans to which the public is ready to respond, and speak in the language of the audience to obtain favorable reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve as purveyor of news that satisfies editors' needs
rubrics_metrics.description: To the newspaper the public relations counsel serves as a purveyor of news. A paper may succeed without editorials worth reading ... but it cannot possibly thrive unless it gets the news and prints it in a pleasing and attractive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide news that is inherently interesting, timely, and presented in an attractive form; understand newspapers' commercial and psychological craving for news (illustrated by the San Francisco 1906 example). Tailor releases so editors find them printable and appealing to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align campaigns with favorable timing and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed conditions can make possible modifications in the public point of view ... The campaign [by savings banks] was successful ... because inflation made it easy for the public to see the wisdom of the doctrines preached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule and frame campaigns when external conditions increase public receptivity (economic, social, political), and call attention to these conditions in messaging to magnify persuasive impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse and ethical misuse of devices
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one danger in the use of stereotypes by the public relations counsel. That is, by the substitution of words for acts, demagogues in every field ... can take advantage of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ethical limits: avoid hollow slogans, overused stereotypes ('Hundred per cent American' died from over use), and manipulative substitutions that mislead the public. Balance efficacy with responsibility to prevent suppression or oppression.
